opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about a lot. When people scale up inference-time compute, a very common recipe is to sample many reasoning traces in parallel, then aggregate them with majority voting, a verifier, or best-of-n selection. The implicit assumption is that the samples will be meaningfully different from each other. In practice, they often aren't. Models tend to collapse onto a small number of modes, especially after post-training. So you might sample a hundred chains of thought and find that they're really just a handful of approaches with superficial variation. That's wasted compute.

The naive fix is to turn up the temperature, and that does give you diversity, but it's uncontrolled. You get token-level noise rather than different strategies. The reasoning starts to degrade: arithmetic errors, incoherent steps, drifting off task. So you're trading quality for diversity in a really inefficient way.

What we actually want is diversity at the level of ideas or strategies, while each individual trace stays high quality. One trace might try a direct algebraic approach, another might work backwards, another might look for a counterexample. That's the controlled part: the variation should be structured and meaningful, not random.

There are a few ways to get there. One is to intervene at the start of generation. A lot of the downstream variation is determined by the first few decisions, so if you diversify the opening moves, like the plan or the framing, and then let the model decode fairly confidently from there, you get much better coverage than spreading randomness uniformly across every token. Another is to condition explicitly on different strategies or hints, so the parallel threads are steered into different regions of the solution space. And there's a training-side angle too. Standard fine-tuning objectives tend to reward the model for putting all its mass on the single most likely answer, which kills diversity. You can design objectives that keep the model's distribution over approaches broader, so it remains a good proposal distribution for search at test time.

The bigger conceptual point is that once you do a lot of inference-time search, the thing you care about isn't really pass@1 anymore. It's something like pass@k: does the set of attempts cover the right answer? Those two goals can actually be in tension. A model that is very sharp on pass@1 can be worse at pass@k because it's lost its exploratory breadth. So we need to think about training and decoding jointly, with the downstream aggregation strategy in mind, rather than optimizing each piece in isolation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that diversity at inference time is really a property of the model, not just of the sampling procedure. People tend to treat it as a knob you turn — raise the temperature, add some nucleus sampling, run eight chains instead of one — and you get more variety. But what we've been finding is that the kind of diversity you actually want, where the parallel lines of thought are genuinely exploring different hypotheses or different solution strategies, is something the model either has or doesn't have, and a lot of it gets shaped during training.

So the way I think about it is in terms of what you might call the "effective support" of the model's distribution. If you take a base model and look at the set of plausible reasoning paths it can produce for a hard problem, that set is often quite rich. Then you do post-training, you do RL with verifiable rewards, and what tends to happen is the distribution collapses. The model gets very good at one mode, and when you sample multiple times you get what look like paraphrases of the same reasoning rather than real alternatives. So you're paying the compute cost of parallelism without getting the benefit.

Now, "controlled" is the important word in your question, because uncontrolled diversity is easy and useless. If I just crank up the temperature, I get lots of garbage. What I want is diversity on the dimensions that matter — the high-level plan, which lemma to try first, which decomposition of the problem — while keeping the low-level execution tight and correct. And those are different things. A lot of the noise from temperature sampling lands on token-level choices that don't change the semantic content at all, or it lands in places where variation just produces errors.

So a few directions we've been pursuing. One is at the training level: can you shape the RL objective so that you don't collapse? There's a tension here, because the thing that makes RL work — reinforcing successful trajectories — is exactly the thing that narrows the distribution. Rewarding only correctness is what pushes you toward a single mode. So you need some notion of reward or regularization that explicitly values coverage of the solution space, not just success on any one sample. If I'm going to generate N paths, the objective I actually care about is something like pass-at-N, not expected single-sample accuracy, and those have quite different optima.

The second direction is more structural. Instead of relying on randomness to produce diversity, you condition the parallel branches on different things. You give each branch a different prefix, a different framing of the problem, or you explicitly ask the model to generate an approach that is different from the ones it's already proposed. That's more controllable, but it raises its own questions, because the model's ability to follow "give me something different" is itself a capability that may or may not be reliable, especially after post-training.

And I think the third thing, which is where some of my interest in robustness comes in, is that you need to be careful about what you're diversifying over. If the model has a systematic blind spot — some concept it just doesn't represent well — then no amount of sampling is going to get you out of that. The parallel branches will all share the blind spot. So diversity at inference time can give you a false sense of coverage. You see twenty different-looking paths and conclude you've explored the space, but actually they're twenty projections of the same underlying limitation. That's where I'd say it's really important to measure diversity semantically rather than just at the surface, and to be honest about whether the variation you're seeing corresponds to genuinely different hypotheses.

So, the short version: controlled diversity is something you have to engineer into the model rather than bolt on at sampling time, and the most useful framing I've found is to ask, "What is the objective I actually care about at inference time?" and then work backwards from that to the training procedure.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: diversity in what space? If you just increase the temperature, you can get outputs that look different but are making essentially the same argument, or you can get outputs that are simply less useful. Neither necessarily gives you the benefit you want from parallel reasoning.

What you’d really like is diversity in the approaches being explored. Maybe one line of thought tries to construct a solution, another looks for a counterexample, and another works through a simpler special case. You’re giving the model different directions while keeping them anchored to the same problem.

Then there’s a selection problem. If one of those branches finds something useful, can you recognize it? For a task where you can check the answer, that’s much easier. For an open-ended question, generating more perspectives doesn’t automatically tell you which perspective to trust.

So I’d think about exploration and verification together. The goal isn’t just to make the branches different; it’s to make them usefully complementary, and to have a way of turning that exploration into a better final answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that diversity by itself isn’t the goal. You want diversity that increases the chance of finding a correct solution. If you sample ten different chains of thought, they might look different on the surface but all make the same underlying mistake.

So one way to think about controlled diversity is: what do you want the different branches to explore? You might have them start from different assumptions, try different decompositions, or use different solution strategies. That gives you a more meaningful kind of diversity than simply turning up the temperature.

And then you need a way to use those branches. Can you reliably recognize a good answer? Can one branch identify a mistake in another? If your selection mechanism can’t distinguish correct reasoning from plausible reasoning, generating more candidates may not help very much.

So I would think about the generation and selection mechanisms together. Under a fixed inference budget, how much should you spend exploring different approaches, and how much should you spend checking them? The useful measure is whether those additional lines of thought contribute something that the others missed.
